title: Research Data and Repositories
answer: FAIR data, metadata and ontologies, federated sharing, institutional knowledge graphs and long-term preservation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR data describes research outputs that are findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable by both people and machines.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies give research data repositories the descriptive structure needed to make datasets findable, comparable, and reusable across disciplines.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers methods for research institutions to jointly analyze or train models on restricted datasets without moving raw records to a central repository.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organization's entities, documents, people, projects, datasets, and their relationships, maintained by a university, library, or research institute.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation is the set of policies, technologies and practices that keep research data and repository objects readable, usable and authentic for decades or longer.

sections.body: This field covers how research data is described, shared, connected and kept usable over time. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work here, such as extracting structured metadata from papers and datasets, linking entities to controlled vocabularies, and suggesting ontology alignments. In federated settings, AI models help match queries across institutions without moving raw data, and they assist with de-identification of sensitive records. For institutional knowledge graphs, machine learning populates nodes and edges from publication records, grant data and internal project descriptions. In preservation, AI is used to detect file format obsolescence and to generate technical metadata for archived software and models.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. FAIR data principles are widely accepted, but actual compliance is often shallow because metadata fields remain incomplete or inconsistent. Ontology construction still depends heavily on human domain experts, and automated alignment between different vocabularies is only reliable for well-studied fields. Federated sharing of sensitive data has working prototypes in clinical and administrative research, but governance, consent and audit trails remain hard problems that no general tool solves. Institutional knowledge graphs tend to be partial and quickly out of date unless a dedicated team maintains them. Long-term digital preservation of AI artifacts is not solved, because models depend on specific software libraries, training data and compute environments that are rarely archived together.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with FAIR Data to understand the four principles that the other pages assume. Metadata and Ontologies then explains the descriptive layer that makes FAIR data searchable and comparable. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data builds on that layer by showing how institutions can answer queries across separate repositories without centralizing personal or confidential records. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows one way an organization can combine its own publications, people and projects into a queryable structure, drawing on the metadata practices from the earlier pages. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the section by addressing whether any of this remains readable and usable years later, which is a separate problem from sharing it today.
